title: Chapter 11.  Wars & Conflicts — 1965, 1971 & the Kargil War of 1999

blocks.content: Beyond the First Kashmir War covered in Chapter 8, J&K has been the direct theatre or a major factor in three further India-Pakistan conflicts — each generating its own set of frequently tested facts, dates, and military/diplomatic outcomes.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The 1965 conflict represented the Second Kashmir War between India and Pakistan over Jammu & Kashmir.
The 1971 War had significant dimensions along the J&K border alongside the Eastern front.
The Kargil War of 1999 was a high-altitude conflict focused on clearing Pakistani infiltrators along the Line of Control.
These conflicts led to major bilateral agreements such as the Tashkent Declaration (1966) and the Shimla Agreement (1972).

blocks.content: The 1965 India-Pakistan War began with Pakistan's 'Operation Gibraltar' — an attempt to infiltrate armed personnel into Indian-administered Kashmir to incite a local uprising against Indian rule, which failed to achieve its intended popular support and was detected and repelled by Indian forces.

Following this, full-scale conventional war broke out between India and Pakistan in August-September 1965, fought across both the J&K front and the international border further south (notably in the Punjab/Sialkot sector), ending in a UN-mandated ceasefire in September 1965.

The war was formally concluded by the Tashkent Declaration (January 1966), brokered by the Soviet Union, under which both countries agreed to withdraw to pre-war positions — Indian Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri died in Tashkent shortly after signing the agreement, an event that remains a significant and sometimes controversial moment in Indian political history.

★ EXAM POINT: Operation Gibraltar (1965) — Pakistan's failed infiltration attempt intended to spark a Kashmiri uprising — directly parallels, in strategic logic, the later Kargil intrusion of 1999; both relied on the (mistaken) expectation of local support or plausible deniability, making this a useful comparative theme across the two conflicts.
Wars & Conflicts — 1965, 1971 & the Kargil War of 1999

The 1971 India-Pakistan War was primarily fought over the crisis in East Pakistan (leading to the creation of Bangladesh), but it also included significant fighting along the J&K front, where Indian forces made territorial gains in certain sectors.

The war concluded with the Simla Agreement (2 July 1972), signed by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and Pakistani President Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, which — critically for J&K's geography (see Chapter 1) — formally renamed and re-designated the erstwhile Ceasefire Line as the 'Line of Control' (LoC), with both countries agreeing to resolve differences bilaterally and to respect the LoC without prejudice to their respective positions on the underlying dispute.

★ EXAM POINT: The Simla Agreement (2 July 1972) is the direct legal source of the term 'Line of Control' — before 1972, the same boundary was called the Ceasefire Line (established 1 January 1949, per Chapter 8). Remember this exact renaming event and date, as it is very frequently tested.

rows: Operation Vijay Success / Restoration of LoC

blocks.content: In the winter of 1998-99, Pakistani soldiers and paramilitary personnel (initially presented by Pakistan as 'freedom fighters'/local militants, though later widely acknowledged to include regular Pakistani Army personnel) covertly occupied strategic high-altitude positions vacated seasonally by Indian troops on the Indian side of the LoC in the Kargil sector, aiming to sever the vital Srinagar-Leh highway (National Highway 1) and internationalise the Kashmir dispute.

India launched 'Operation Vijay' (a different operation from the 1961 Goa annexation operation of the same name, covered in the DNH&DD chapter of the companion volume on that UT) to evict the intruders, involving intense high-altitude combat — much of it above 16,000-18,000 feet — across peaks including Tololing and Tiger Hill, through May-July 1999.

The Indian Air Force also conducted air strikes in support of ground operations ('Operation Safed Sagar'), and the conflict concluded with a full Indian recapture of the intruded positions by July 1999, following international diplomatic pressure (notably from the United States) on Pakistan to withdraw.

Kargil Vijay Diwas is commemorated annually on 26 July, marking the formal declaration of the conflict's end and India's recapture of all Kargil-sector heights; the Kargil War Memorial at Dras honours the Indian soldiers who died in the conflict.

items: Operation Vijay was the official Indian military campaign to reclaim heights in the Kargil war of 1999.
The 1972 Shimla Agreement re-designated the 1949 Ceasefire Line as the Line of Control (LoC).
Questions frequently test post-war diplomatic accords: Tashkent Declaration (1966) vs. Shimla Agreement (1972).

cells: Operation Vijay (ground); Operation Safed Sagar (Indian Air Force component)
Tololing, Tiger Hill, and other high-altitude peaks in the Kargil-Dras sector

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Do NOT confuse the 1999 Kargil War's 'Operation Vijay' with the 1961 'Operation Vijay' used for the Indian annexation of Goa, Daman and Diu — both share the same codename but refer to entirely different military operations 38 years apart, a very frequently tested trap across multiple UT/state syllabi.

items: 1965 War: began with Pakistan's failed 'Operation Gibraltar' infiltration; ended with the Tashkent Declaration (Jan 1966), brokered by the USSR.
1971 War: concluded by the Simla Agreement (2 July 1972), which renamed the Ceasefire Line as the Line of Control (LoC).
Kargil War (1999): Indian operation codenamed 'Operation Vijay' (ground) + 'Operation Safed Sagar' (IAF); key battles at Tololing and Tiger Hill.
Kargil Vijay Diwas commemorated annually on 26 July; Kargil War Memorial located at Dras.
1999's 'Operation Vijay' (Kargil) is distinct from 1961's 'Operation Vijay' (Goa annexation) — same name, different operations.
